Troubleshooting

Source: vignettes/articles/troubleshooting.Rmd
troubleshooting.Rmd

This article explains common errors and unexpected results when preparing sensor records, fitting models and predicting new observations. Each example shows the message, its cause and a working call.

The examples use 24 study plots, each with hourly soil-temperature readings for 60 days from 1 September 2021, and two species whose presence depends on each plot’s average warmth. A plot is a unit. Readings are grouped into time intervals called bins, and the interval length, such as a week or month, is the grain. A learner specifies the model to fit; its combination with a particular input summary is a candidate.

Installation 

# Install from CRAN
install.packages("timesift")

# Or install the development version from GitHub
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/timesift")
# Install from PyPI
pip install timesift

# with the torch encoders, the contrasts and the plots
pip install "timesift[torch,contrasts,plot]"

# Or install the development version from GitHub
pip install git+https://github.com/gcol33/timesift

The Python block draws its own record, so the values it prints differ from the ones quoted in the text, which come from the R run. Counts, shapes and calendar boundaries do not depend on the draw and agree.

hours <- seq(as.POSIXct("2021-09-01", tz = "UTC"), by = "hour", length.out = 24 * 60)
ids <- sprintf("p%02d", 1:24)
warmth <- rnorm(24)

series <- data.frame(
  plot = rep(ids, each = length(hours)),
  t = rep(hours, times = 24),
  temp = as.numeric(vapply(warmth, function(w) {
    w + 5 * sin(seq_along(hours) / 200) + rnorm(length(hours), sd = 3)
  }, numeric(length(hours))))
)
targets <- data.frame(plot = ids,
                      sp1 = rbinom(24, 1, plogis(2 * warmth)),
                      sp2 = rbinom(24, 1, plogis(-2 * warmth)))
colSums(targets[c("sp1", "sp2")])
#> sp1 sp2 
#>  14  10
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import timesift as ts

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
hours = pd.date_range("2021-09-01", periods=24 * 60, freq="h")
ids = [f"p{i:02d}" for i in range(1, 25)]
warmth = rng.normal(size=24)

series = pd.DataFrame({
    "plot": np.repeat(ids, len(hours)),
    "t": np.tile(hours, 24),
    "temp": np.concatenate([
        w + 5 * np.sin(np.arange(1, len(hours) + 1) / 200) + rng.normal(scale=3, size=len(hours))
        for w in warmth]),
})
targets = pd.DataFrame({"plot": ids,
                        "sp1": rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-2 * warmth))),
                        "sp2": rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(2 * warmth)))})
targets[["sp1", "sp2"]].sum()
#> sp1    13
#> sp2    15
#> dtype: int64

A unit has no readings in a bin

A logger that was stolen for a week, or one that started late, leaves a hole in the record. Here plot p03 loses the calendar week beginning Monday 13 September.

lost <- series$plot == "p03" &
  series$t >= as.POSIXct("2021-09-13", tz = "UTC") &
  series$t < as.POSIXct("2021-09-20", tz = "UTC")
gappy <- series[!lost, ]

grain_matrix(gappy, plot, t, temp, grain = "week")
#> Error:
#> ! 1 (unit, bin) cell holds no readings, first: unit p03 at 2021-09-13T00:00:00. Every unit must span every bin; gaps are not padded. coverage() lists them.
lost = ((series["plot"] == "p03") & (series["t"] >= "2021-09-13")
        & (series["t"] < "2021-09-20"))
gappy = series[~lost]

ts.grain_matrix(gappy, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week")
#> ValueError: 1 (unit, bin) cell holds no readings, first: unit p03 at 2021-09-13T00:00:00. Every unit must span every bin; gaps are not padded. coverage() lists them.

Every unit needs at least one reading in every bin. An empty bin has no summary value, so timesift() raises an error when building the arrays. Any interpolation or imputation must be chosen and applied before fitting.

coverage() lays out the same binning as a count of readings per unit and bin, so the gaps can be found before deciding what to do about them.

cov <- coverage(gappy, plot, t, grain = "week")
cov
#> <timesift coverage> 24 units x 9 bins at the week grain
#> 1 empty (unit, bin) cell in 1 unit: p03
cov["p03", ]
#> 2021-08-30T00:00:00Z 2021-09-06T00:00:00Z 2021-09-13T00:00:00Z 
#>                  120                  168                    0 
#> 2021-09-20T00:00:00Z 2021-09-27T00:00:00Z 2021-10-04T00:00:00Z 
#>                  168                  168                  168 
#> 2021-10-11T00:00:00Z 2021-10-18T00:00:00Z 2021-10-25T00:00:00Z 
#>                  168                  168                  144
cov = ts.coverage(gappy, "plot", "t", grain="week")
cov
#> <timesift coverage> 24 units x 9 bins at the week grain
#> 1 empty (unit, bin) cells in 1 units: p03
pd.Series(cov.count[cov.units.index("p03")], index=cov.bins)
#> 2021-08-30T00:00:00Z    120
#> 2021-09-06T00:00:00Z    168
#> 2021-09-13T00:00:00Z      0
#> 2021-09-20T00:00:00Z    168
#> 2021-09-27T00:00:00Z    168
#> 2021-10-04T00:00:00Z    168
#> 2021-10-11T00:00:00Z    168
#> 2021-10-18T00:00:00Z    168
#> 2021-10-25T00:00:00Z    144
#> dtype: int32

You can exclude units with incomplete records, restrict the period to dates covered by every unit, or choose a coarser grain with readings in every bin. Here monthly bins work because p03 still has readings in September.

dim(grain_matrix(gappy[gappy$plot != "p03", ], plot, t, temp, grain = "week"))
#> [1] 23  9  1
dim(grain_matrix(gappy, plot, t, temp, grain = "month"))
#> [1] 24  2  1
ts.grain_matrix(gappy[gappy["plot"] != "p03"], "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week").shape
#> (23, 9, 1)
ts.grain_matrix(gappy, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="month").shape
#> (24, 2, 1)

A week missing from every unit at once is refused under a different message, because the gap is then a bin that no unit reaches. Dropping that bin silently would make the weeks either side of it look adjacent.

everyone <- series$t >= as.POSIXct("2021-09-13", tz = "UTC") &
  series$t < as.POSIXct("2021-09-20", tz = "UTC")
grain_matrix(series[!everyone, ], plot, t, temp, grain = "week")
#> Error:
#> ! the week bins are not contiguous: nothing falls in the one beginning 2021-09-13T00:00:00, between 2021-09-06T00:00:00 and 2021-09-20T00:00:00. Bins must tile the record; a gap is not closed up.
everyone = (series["t"] >= "2021-09-13") & (series["t"] < "2021-09-20")
ts.grain_matrix(series[~everyone], "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week")
#> ValueError: the week bins are not contiguous: nothing falls in the one beginning 2021-09-13T00:00:00, between 2021-09-06T00:00:00 and 2021-09-20T00:00:00. Bins must tile the record; a gap is not closed up.

The first and last bins are partial

1 September 2021 was a Wednesday, so the first weekly bin begins on Monday 30 August, two days before the record does, and the last week runs past its end.

x <- grain_matrix(series, plot, t, temp, grain = "week")
dimnames(x)[[2]]
#> [1] "2021-08-30T00:00:00Z" "2021-09-06T00:00:00Z" "2021-09-13T00:00:00Z"
#> [4] "2021-09-20T00:00:00Z" "2021-09-27T00:00:00Z" "2021-10-04T00:00:00Z"
#> [7] "2021-10-11T00:00:00Z" "2021-10-18T00:00:00Z" "2021-10-25T00:00:00Z"
attr(x, "bin_partial")
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
attr(x, "bin_n")[1, ]
#> 2021-08-30T00:00:00Z 2021-09-06T00:00:00Z 2021-09-13T00:00:00Z 
#>                  120                  168                  168 
#> 2021-09-20T00:00:00Z 2021-09-27T00:00:00Z 2021-10-04T00:00:00Z 
#>                  168                  168                  168 
#> 2021-10-11T00:00:00Z 2021-10-18T00:00:00Z 2021-10-25T00:00:00Z 
#>                  168                  168                  144
x = ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week")
x.bins
#> ('2021-08-30T00:00:00Z', '2021-09-06T00:00:00Z', '2021-09-13T00:00:00Z', '2021-09-20T00:00:00Z', '2021-09-27T00:00:00Z', '2021-10-04T00:00:00Z', '2021-10-11T00:00:00Z', '2021-10-18T00:00:00Z', '2021-10-25T00:00:00Z')
x.bin_partial
#> array([ True, False, False, False, False, False, False, False,  True])
x.bin_n[0]
#> array([120, 168, 168, 168, 168, 168, 168, 168, 144], dtype=int32)

Weekly intervals start on Monday. The record begins on Wednesday, so the first week contains fewer readings. bin_partial marks incomplete intervals and bin_n counts their readings: 120 in the first week and 168 in a full week. A partial bin’s mean and daily extremes are calculated from the readings available in that interval.

partial = "drop" removes them.

dim(grain_matrix(series, plot, t, temp, grain = "week", partial = "drop"))
#> [1] 24  7  1
ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week", partial="drop").shape
#> (24, 7, 1)

On a grain coarser than the record, dropping can leave nothing, and that is an error.

grain_matrix(series, plot, t, temp, grain = "season", partial = "drop")
#> Error:
#> ! dropping the partial bins leaves no bin: the record covers no whole season. Use `partial = "keep"` or a finer grain.
ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="season", partial="drop")
#> ValueError: dropping the partial bins leaves no bin: the record covers no whole season. Use partial='keep' or a finer grain.

timesift() keeps partial bins, because dropping them throws away the ends of the record: on a seasonal grain that can be three months at each end. To fit on whole bins alone, cut the series to the bin boundaries before the call. Monday 6 September to Sunday 24 October is seven whole weeks.

whole <- series[series$t >= as.POSIXct("2021-09-06", tz = "UTC") &
                  series$t < as.POSIXct("2021-10-25", tz = "UTC"), ]
attr(grain_matrix(whole, plot, t, temp, grain = "week"), "bin_partial")
#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
whole = series[(series["t"] >= "2021-09-06") & (series["t"] < "2021-10-25")]
ts.grain_matrix(whole, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week").bin_partial
#> array([False, False, False, False, False, False, False])

The time column is not POSIXct, or sits in an unexpected zone

A time column read from a CSV file arrives as text, and one built with as.Date() has lost its hours. Both are refused.

as_text <- transform(series, t = format(t))
grain_matrix(as_text, plot, t, temp, grain = "day")
#> Error:
#> ! `t` must be POSIXct, not character.

as_date <- transform(series, t = as.Date(t))
grain_matrix(as_date, plot, t, temp, grain = "day")
#> Error:
#> ! `t` must be POSIXct, not Date.

The fix is to parse the column with its zone stated, for example as.POSIXct(x, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC"). A zone name the zone database does not know is refused too, since reading a clock in it would fall back to UTC with only a warning.

odd <- series
attr(odd$t, "tzone") <- "CET+1"
grain_matrix(odd, plot, t, temp, grain = "day")
#> Error:
#> ! `t` is carried in the time zone "CET+1", which the zone database does not know. Name one of `OlsonNames()`.
ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="day", tz="CET+1")
#> ZoneInfoNotFoundError: 'No time zone found with key CET+1'

The surprise that raises no error is the zone itself. Bins follow the calendar of the tzone attribute, so the same instants carried in "Europe/Vienna" are cut into days at Vienna’s midnight, which in September is 22:00 UTC.

In Python the calendar is named by tz, or by the zone a time column carries.

vienna <- series
attr(vienna$t, "tzone") <- "Europe/Vienna"
xv <- grain_matrix(vienna, plot, t, temp, grain = "day")
dimnames(xv)[[2]][1:2]
#> [1] "2021-08-31T22:00:00Z" "2021-09-01T22:00:00Z"
attr(xv, "bin_partial")[1:2]
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
attr(xv, "bin_n")[1, 1:2]
#> 2021-08-31T22:00:00Z 2021-09-01T22:00:00Z 
#>                   22                   24
xv = ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="day", tz="Europe/Vienna")
xv.bins[:2]
#> ('2021-08-31T22:00:00Z', '2021-09-01T22:00:00Z')
xv.bin_partial[:2]
#> array([ True, False])
xv.bin_n[0, :2]
#> array([22, 24], dtype=int32)

The first Vienna day began two hours before the first reading, so it is partial and holds 22 readings. In a zone that keeps daylight saving time the day the clock goes forward holds 23 hours and the day it goes back 25. A record kept on a fixed offset bins into days of 24 hours once its tzone names that offset, such as "Etc/GMT-1" for Central European standard time. The zone is a decision about what a day means for the question, and it is worth setting explicitly.

fixed <- series
attr(fixed$t, "tzone") <- "Etc/GMT-1"
dimnames(grain_matrix(fixed, plot, t, temp, grain = "day"))[[2]][1:2]
#> [1] "2021-08-31T23:00:00Z" "2021-09-01T23:00:00Z"
ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="day", tz="Etc/GMT-1").bins[:2]
#> ('2021-08-31T23:00:00Z', '2021-09-01T23:00:00Z')

On that offset every day begins at 23:00 UTC, in summer and in winter alike.

Missing readings and repeated instants

A reading that is NA and an instant recorded twice for the same unit are both refused where the record is read.

holed <- series
holed$temp[5] <- NA
grain_matrix(holed, plot, t, temp, grain = "day")
#> Error:
#> ! 1 reading is not a finite number, first: unit p01 at 2021-09-01T04:00:00. Fill or drop it before building a representation.

grain_matrix(rbind(series, series[1, ]), plot, t, temp, grain = "day")
#> Error:
#> ! 1 duplicated (unit, time) pair, first: p01 at 2021-09-01T00:00:00Z.
holed = series.copy()
holed.loc[4, "temp"] = np.nan
ts.grain_matrix(holed, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="day")
#> ValueError: 1 reading is not a finite number, first: unit p01 at 2021-09-01T04:00:00. Fill or drop it before building a representation.
ts.grain_matrix(pd.concat([series, series.iloc[[0]]]), "plot", "t", "temp", grain="day")
#> ValueError: 1 duplicated (unit, time) pair, first: p01 at 2021-09-01T00:00:00Z.

A logger that wrote the same hour twice usually did so around a download or a clock change. Removing the repeated rows, or keeping one per instant on a rule that suits the logger, comes before any representation.

Targets and series carry different units

targets and series are linked by the column id names. A target whose unit has no record is refused, naming the units.

extra <- rbind(targets, data.frame(plot = c("p98", "p99"), sp1 = 1, sp2 = 0))
timesift(extra, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t, verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! 2 targets name a unit `series` does not carry: p98, p99.
extra = pd.concat([targets, pd.DataFrame({"plot": ["p98", "p99"], "sp1": 1, "sp2": 0})],
                  ignore_index=True)
ts.timesift(extra, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t", verbose=False)
#> ValueError: 2 targets name a unit the series does not carry, first: p98.

series may contain additional units. Only units identified in targets enter the fit.

fewer <- targets[-(1:2), ]
fit_fewer <- timesift(fewer, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                      sift = grains("week"), resampling = cv(v = 3), n_inner = NULL,
                      ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
dim(fit_fewer$y)
#> [1] 22  2
fewer = targets.iloc[2:]
fit_fewer = ts.timesift(fewer, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                        sift=ts.grains("week"), resampling=ts.cv(v=3), n_inner=None,
                        ensemble=False, verbose=False)
fit_fewer.y.values.shape
#> (22, 2)

The fit holds 22 targets, although the series carries 24 plots. When a plot seems to be missing from the results, rownames(fit$y) lists the targets that were fitted.

Two rows of targets with one identifier are refused unless target_time says where in time each row sits, because otherwise both rows would read the same record.

timesift(rbind(targets, targets[1, ]), series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
         verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! `targets` holds more than one row for 1 identifier: p01. Give `target_time` to say where in time each row sits.
ts.timesift(pd.concat([targets, targets.iloc[[0]]]), series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            verbose=False)
#> ValueError: 1 id appears in more than one row of `targets`: p01. Give `target_time` to anchor repeated targets in time.

A learner cannot read the representation

Learners accept either a table of predictors or values ordered by time. elasticnet() uses a table. native() keeps every reading as a separate time bin, and the package rejects this representation for tabular learners. Assigning it explicitly through data = raises the error before the array is built.

timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
         learners = elasticnet(data = native()), verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! `elasticnet()` reads a tabular representation; `native()` gives it one column per reading. Use `grain()`, `multigrain()` or `lookback()`.
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            learners=ts.elasticnet(data=ts.native()), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: elasticnet() reads a tabular representation; native gives it one column per reading. Use grain(), multigrain() or lookback().

When the same pair arises from a sift expansion, the run goes ahead without it, says so once, and records why in fit$candidates.

fit_skip <- timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                     sift = c(native(), grain("week")), resampling = cv(v = 3),
                     n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE)
#> skipping 1 candidate no learner can read: elasticnet / native
#> fold 1 of 3, 0 s
#> fold 2 of 3, 0 s
#> fold 3 of 3, 0 s
#> refitting every candidate on all 24 targets
fit_skip$candidates[c("candidate", "status", "note")]
#>             candidate         status
#> 1 elasticnet / native not applicable
#> 2   elasticnet / week         fitted
#>                                                                                                                                        note
#> 1 `elasticnet()` reads a tabular representation; `native()` gives it one column per reading. Use `grain()`, `multigrain()` or `lookback()`.
#> 2                                                                                                                                      <NA>
fit_skip = ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                       sift=[ts.native(), ts.grain("week")], resampling=ts.cv(v=3),
                       n_inner=None, ensemble=False)
#> building the week representation
#> not applicable: elasticnet() reads a tabular representation; native gives it one column per reading. Use grain(), multigrain() or lookback().
#> fold 1 of 3
#> fold 2 of 3
#> fold 3 of 3
#> refitting every candidate on all 24 targets
pd.DataFrame(fit_skip.candidates)[["candidate", "reason"]]
#>              candidate                                             reason
#> 0  elasticnet / native  elasticnet() reads a tabular representation; n...
#> 1    elasticnet / week

If no pair in the run can be fitted, the run stops and lists every reason.

timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t, sift = native(),
         verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! no learner can read any representation in the sift:
#>   `elasticnet()` reads a tabular representation; `native()` gives it one column per reading. Use `grain()`, `multigrain()` or `lookback()`.
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t", sift=ts.native(), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: no learner can read any of the representations:
#>   elasticnet() reads a tabular representation; native gives it one column per reading. Use grain(), multigrain() or lookback().

The sequence learners, cnn() and rescnn(), are refused the opposite case: a multigrain() is a flat block of features with no order to convolve along, and a grain the record holds only one bin of is a sequence of length one. The first is refused before the record is read, the second once the array says how many bins it has. Neither needs torch to be refused.

timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
         learners = cnn(data = multigrain(c("week", "month"))), verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! `cnn()` reads a sequence; `multigrain()` gives one row of features.

timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
         learners = cnn(data = grain("year")), verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! `cnn()` reads a sequence; `grain("year")` gives one row of features.
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            learners=ts.cnn(data=ts.multigrain(("week", "month"))), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: no learner can read any of the representations:
#>   cnn() reads a sequence; multigrain(week+month) gives one row of 11 features
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            learners=ts.cnn(data=ts.grain("year")), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: no learner can read any of the representations:
#>   cnn() reads a sequence; year gives one row of 1 features

A learner’s data = names a representation outside the sift

A learner given data = is fitted on that representation alone, and the run builds it whether or not the sift holds it. Here the forest reads months while the elastic net runs across the sift.

fit_pin <- timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                    learners = c(elasticnet(), forest(data = grain("month"))),
                    sift = grains("week"), resampling = cv(v = 3), n_inner = NULL,
                    ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
fit_pin$candidates[c("candidate", "representation", "bins")]
#>           candidate representation bins
#> 1 elasticnet / week           week    9
#> 2    forest / month          month    2
fit_pin = ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                      learners=[ts.elasticnet(), ts.forest(data=ts.grain("month"))],
                      sift=ts.grains("week"), resampling=ts.cv(v=3), n_inner=None,
                      ensemble=False, verbose=False)
pd.DataFrame(fit_pin.candidates)[["candidate", "representation", "bins"]]
#>            candidate representation  bins
#> 0  elasticnet / week           week     9
#> 1     forest / month          month     2

The error comes when the pinned representation and one in the sift would be reported under the same name but differ in their settings, such as the weekly mean in the sift and the weekly extremes for the forest.

timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
         learners = c(elasticnet(),
                      forest(data = grain("week", stats = c("cold_day", "warm_day")))),
         sift = grains("week"), verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! two representations are reported under the name "week": the one the forest learner is pinned to and the one in the sift. Name the sift to tell them apart.
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            learners=[ts.elasticnet(),
                      ts.forest(data=ts.grain("week", stats=("cold_day", "warm_day")))],
            sift=ts.grains("week"), verbose=False)
#> ValueError: two representations are reported under the name "week": the one the forest learner is pinned to and the one in the sift. Name the sift to tell them apart.

Give the representation in sift a distinct name so that the two candidates can be identified separately.

fit_named <- timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                      learners = c(elasticnet(),
                                   forest(data = grain("week", stats = c("cold_day", "warm_day")))),
                      sift = list(week_mean = grain("week")), resampling = cv(v = 3),
                      n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
fit_named$candidates[c("candidate", "channels")]
#>                candidate channels
#> 1 elasticnet / week_mean        1
#> 2          forest / week        2
fit_named = ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                        learners=[ts.elasticnet(),
                                  ts.forest(data=ts.grain("week", stats=("cold_day", "warm_day")))],
                        sift={"week_mean": ts.grain("week")}, resampling=ts.cv(v=3),
                        n_inner=None, ensemble=False, verbose=False)
pd.DataFrame(fit_named.candidates)[["candidate", "channels"]]
#>                 candidate  channels
#> 0  elasticnet / week_mean         1
#> 1           forest / week         2

Day-level statistics at a sub-daily grain

cold_day, warm_day, mean_daily_min and mean_daily_max first reduce each day to one number, so they need bins of a day or longer. The refusal comes from the constructor, before any data are read.

grain("halfday", stats = c("mean", "cold_day"))
#> Error:
#> ! `halfday` bins are shorter than a day, so cold_day is not defined there. Use a grain of `day` or coarser.
ts.grain("halfday", stats=("mean", "cold_day"))
#> ValueError: `halfday` bins are shorter than a day, so cold_day is not defined there. Use a grain of `day` or coarser.

The coldest single reading of a half-day bin is min, and the coldest day is defined from the "day" grain upward.

grain("halfday", stats = c("mean", "min"))
#> <timesift representation> halfday 
#> kind    : grain (a sequence) 
#> grain   : halfday 
#> stats   : mean, min
grain("week", stats = c("cold_day", "mean", "warm_day"))
#> <timesift representation> week 
#> kind    : grain (a sequence) 
#> grain   : week 
#> stats   : cold_day, mean, warm_day
ts.grain("halfday", stats=("mean", "min"))
#> <timesift representation> halfday
#> kind    : grain (a sequence)
#> grain   : halfday
#> stats   : mean, min
ts.grain("week", stats=("cold_day", "mean", "warm_day"))
#> <timesift representation> week
#> kind    : grain (a sequence)
#> grain   : week
#> stats   : cold_day, mean, warm_day

A response has too few presences to score

Cross-validation divides plots into groups called folds, then predicts each fold using models trained on the others. To score a species in a test fold, that fold must contain both presences and absences. A model fitted separately for the species also needs both in its training set. A species-fold pair is called a cell. Below, sp3 occurs on two plots and sp4 on none.

rare <- targets
rare$sp3 <- c(1, 1, rep(0, 22))
rare$sp4 <- 0
fit_rare <- timesift(rare, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                     sift = grains("week"), resampling = cv(v = 4), n_inner = NULL,
                     ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
fit_rare$cells
#> <timesift cells> 16 cells over 4 variables 
#> scorable: 8 (50.0%); variables with at least one scorable fold: 2 of 4
cells <- as.data.frame(fit_rare$cells)
cells[cells$variable == "sp3", ]
#>    variable fold n_occ pres_train abs_train pres_test abs_test scorable
#> 9       sp3    1     2          2        16         0        6    FALSE
#> 10      sp3    2     2          2        16         0        6    FALSE
#> 11      sp3    3     2          0        18         2        4    FALSE
#> 12      sp3    4     2          2        16         0        6    FALSE
rare = targets.assign(sp3=[1, 1] + [0] * 22, sp4=0)
fit_rare = ts.timesift(rare, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                       sift=ts.grains("week"), resampling=ts.cv(v=4), n_inner=None,
                       ensemble=False, verbose=False)
from dataclasses import asdict

fit_rare.cells
#> <timesift cells> 16 cells over 4 variables
#> scorable: 8 (50.0%); variables with at least one scorable fold: 2 of 4
cells = pd.DataFrame(asdict(fit_rare.cells))
cells[cells["variable"] == "sp3"]
#>    variable  fold  n_occ  pres_train  abs_train  pres_test  abs_test  scorable
#> 8       sp3     1      2           2         16          0         6     False
#> 9       sp3     2      2           2         16          0         6     False
#> 10      sp3     3      2           2         16          0         6     False
#> 11      sp3     4      2           0         18          2         4     False

In folds 1, 2 and 4 both presences of sp3 sit on the training side, leaving no presence to score, and in fold 3 both are held out, leaving none to fit on.

In folds 1, 2 and 3 both presences of sp3 sit on the training side, leaving no presence to score, and in fold 4 both are held out, leaving none to fit on.

The run continues using the eligible species-fold pairs. fit$cells lists these pairs, based on the observed responses and fold assignments. Every candidate is scored on the same pairs, and sp3 and sp4 contribute to none of the means here. scorable_cells() calculates this eligibility table before fitting.

y <- as.matrix(rare[c("sp1", "sp2", "sp3", "sp4")])
rownames(y) <- rare$plot
scorable_cells(y, fold_map(y, v = 4))
#> <timesift cells> 16 cells over 4 variables 
#> scorable: 8 (50.0%); variables with at least one scorable fold: 2 of 4
y = ts.Response(rare[["sp1", "sp2", "sp3", "sp4"]].to_numpy(dtype=float), tuple(rare["plot"]),
                ("sp1", "sp2", "sp3", "sp4"))
pd.DataFrame(asdict(ts.scorable_cells(y, ts.fold_map(y, v=4))))
#>    variable  fold  n_occ  pres_train  abs_train  pres_test  abs_test  scorable
#> 0       sp1     1     13          10          8          3         3      True
#> 1       sp1     2     13           8         10          5         1      True
#> 2       sp1     3     13           9          9          4         2      True
#> 3       sp1     4     13          12          6          1         5      True
#> 4       sp2     1     15          11          7          4         2      True
#> 5       sp2     2     15          12          6          3         3      True
#> 6       sp2     3     15          12          6          3         3      True
#> 7       sp2     4     15          10          8          5         1      True
#> 8       sp3     1      2           2         16          0         6     False
#> 9       sp3     2      2           2         16          0         6     False
#> 10      sp3     3      2           2         16          0         6     False
#> 11      sp3     4      2           0         18          2         4     False
#> 12      sp4     1      0           0         18          0         6     False
#> 13      sp4     2      0           0         18          0         6     False
#> 14      sp4     3      0           0         18          0         6     False
#> 15      sp4     4      0           0         18          0         6     False

Fewer folds give a rare response more chance of landing on both sides of each split. Only when no cell at all is scorable does the run stop, as it does for a response absent everywhere.

absent <- data.frame(plot = ids, sp0 = 0)
timesift(absent, series, y = sp0, id = plot, time = t, verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! no (response, fold) cell is scorable under this fold map, so no candidate can be scored: every cell needs both classes on each side of its split. See scorable_cells() for the counts; a rarer response needs fewer folds, or a response present somewhere.
absent = pd.DataFrame({"plot": ids, "sp0": 0})
ts.timesift(absent, series, y="sp0", id="plot", time="t", verbose=False)
#> ValueError: no candidate scored inside the training data of fold 1. Widen the inner folds or drop the variables that cannot be scored.

The response itself must be 0 and 1, with no missing value.

counted <- targets
counted$sp1[1] <- 2
timesift(counted, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t, verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! a presence-absence response must be 0/1 or logical.

unknown <- targets
unknown$sp1[1] <- NA
timesift(unknown, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t, verbose = FALSE)
#> Error:
#> ! the response holds missing values. Fill or drop them before fitting.
counted = targets.copy()
counted.loc[0, "sp1"] = 2
ts.timesift(counted, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t", verbose=False)
#> ValueError: a presence-absence response must be 0/1 or logical
unknown = targets.astype({"sp1": float})
unknown.loc[0, "sp1"] = np.nan
ts.timesift(unknown, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t", verbose=False)
#> ValueError: the response holds missing values

A torch learner without torch

mlp(), cnn() and rescnn() declare that they need torch. Constructing one does not load it, so a learner can be written into a script on a machine without torch; the check runs when the learner is fitted, and stops with

the cnn learner needs torch. Install it with install.packages("torch").

naming the learner. That message is quoted from the source here, since the machine this article was built on has torch installed. There is no fallback to a learner that runs without torch, because two code paths would drift apart. The torch package also installs its own libraries the first time it is used, which is torch’s step and not timesift’s.

predict() on a new record

A calendar grain reads a record by the instants of its bins. A fit made on weeks from 30 August to 25 October expects a new record over the same weeks, and a shorter or later record is refused.

fit <- timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                sift = grains("week", "month"), resampling = cv(v = 3), verbose = FALSE)
fit = ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                  sift=ts.grains("week", "month"), resampling=ts.cv(v=3), verbose=False)
shorter <- series[series$t < as.POSIXct("2021-10-15", tz = "UTC"), ]
predict(fit, targets, shorter)
#> Error:
#> ! the representation predicted on has different channels or bins from the fitted one: 7 bins here and 9 bins in the fit. A calendar grain is read by its bins' instants, so a fit predicts a record over the same period; a lookback reads a span relative to each target and predicts any period.

next_year <- transform(series, t = t + 365 * 86400)
predict(fit, targets, next_year)
#> Error:
#> ! the representation predicted on has different channels or bins from the fitted one: bin 1 is 2022-08-29T00:00:00Z here and 2021-08-30T00:00:00Z in the fit. A calendar grain is read by its bins' instants, so a fit predicts a record over the same period; a lookback reads a span relative to each target and predicts any period.

predict(fit, targets, gappy)
#> Error:
#> ! 1 (unit, bin) cell holds no readings, first: unit p03 at 2021-09-13T00:00:00. Every unit must span every bin; gaps are not padded. coverage() lists them.
shorter = series[series["t"] < "2021-10-15"]
fit.predict(targets, shorter)
#> ValueError: the representation predicted on has different channels or bins from the fitted one: 7 bins here and 9 bins in the fit. A calendar grain is read by its bins' instants, so a fit predicts a record over the same period; a lookback reads a span relative to each target and predicts any period.
next_year = series.assign(t=series["t"] + pd.Timedelta(days=365))
fit.predict(targets, next_year)
#> ValueError: the representation predicted on has different channels or bins from the fitted one: bin 1 is 2022-08-29T00:00:00Z here and 2021-08-30T00:00:00Z in the fit. A calendar grain is read by its bins' instants, so a fit predicts a record over the same period; a lookback reads a span relative to each target and predicts any period.
fit.predict(targets, gappy)
#> ValueError: 1 (unit, bin) cell holds no readings, first: unit p03 at 2021-09-13T00:00:00. Every unit must span every bin; gaps are not padded. coverage() lists them.

The first two are the same mismatch: the bins of the new record are not those the fit was made on. The third is the coverage refusal again, raised while building the new array. A record over the same period predicts, for any subset of the units.

predict(fit, targets[1:3, ], series[series$plot %in% ids[1:3], ])
#>           sp1       sp2
#> p01 0.1745044 0.6128003
#> p02 0.5458671 0.4945805
#> p03 0.1465358 0.6298695
fit.predict(targets.iloc[:3], series[series["plot"].isin(ids[:3])]).round(3)
#> array([[0.523, 0.624],
#>        [0.631, 0.622],
#>        [0.565, 0.624]])

To predict another period, the representation has to be anchored on each target’s own instant rather than on the calendar. That is a lookback(), with target_time naming the column of targets holding the instant.

anchored <- transform(targets, at = as.POSIXct("2021-10-30", tz = "UTC"))
fit_lb <- timesift(anchored, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                   target_time = at, sift = lookbacks("28 days", "56 days"),
                   resampling = cv(v = 3), verbose = FALSE)

later <- transform(anchored, at = at + 365 * 86400)
predict(fit_lb, later[1:3, ], next_year[next_year$plot %in% ids[1:3], ])
#>         sp1       sp2
#> 1 0.1886727 0.6033119
#> 2 0.5668084 0.4835910
#> 3 0.1495701 0.6241430
anchored = targets.assign(at=pd.Timestamp("2021-10-30"))
fit_lb = ts.timesift(anchored, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                     target_time="at", sift=ts.lookbacks("28 days", "56 days"),
                     resampling=ts.cv(v=3), verbose=False)

later = anchored.assign(at=anchored["at"] + pd.Timedelta(days=365))
fit_lb.predict(later.iloc[:3], next_year[next_year["plot"].isin(ids[:3])]).round(3)
#> array([[0.582, 0.613],
#>        [0.656, 0.591],
#>        [0.585, 0.613]])

Runs take longer than expected

With n_inner set, each candidate is cross-validated within each outer training set, then fitted once on that whole training set. This requires v_outer * (n_inner + 1) * candidates fits, plus one final fit per candidate on all targets. n_inner = NULL runs only the outer cross-validation, requiring v_outer * candidates fits before the final refits. It reports candidate scores and omits the performance estimate for selection and combination.

v_outer <- 3
candidates <- 2
c(nested = v_outer * (5 + 1) * candidates + candidates,
  outer_only = v_outer * candidates + candidates)
#>     nested outer_only 
#>         38          8

nested <- system.time(timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                               sift = grains("week", "month"), resampling = cv(v = 3),
                               verbose = FALSE))[["elapsed"]]
outer_only <- system.time(timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
                                   sift = grains("week", "month"), resampling = cv(v = 3),
                                   n_inner = NULL, verbose = FALSE))[["elapsed"]]
c(nested = nested, outer_only = outer_only)
#>     nested outer_only 
#>       0.45       0.11
import time

v_outer = 3
candidates = 2
{"nested": v_outer * (5 + 1) * candidates + candidates,
 "outer_only": v_outer * candidates + candidates}
#> {'nested': 38, 'outer_only': 8}

start = time.perf_counter()
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            sift=ts.grains("week", "month"), resampling=ts.cv(v=3), verbose=False);
nested = time.perf_counter() - start
start = time.perf_counter()
ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
            sift=ts.grains("week", "month"), resampling=ts.cv(v=3), n_inner=None,
            verbose=False);
outer_only = time.perf_counter() - start
nested > outer_only
#> True

On this record the nested run took 0.45 seconds and the run on the outer folds alone 0.11.

Each fit in turn costs what its array costs. A calendar grain has as many columns as bins times statistics, and native() has one bin per reading, so its size follows the record directly.

xn <- grain_matrix(series, plot, t, temp, grain = "native")
dim(xn)
#> [1]   24 1440    1
format(object.size(xn), units = "MB")
#> [1] "0.7 Mb"

# Three years of hourly readings on 894 plots, one channel, in megabytes
894 * (3 * 365 + 1) * 24 * 8 / 2^20
#> [1] 179.4111
xn = ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="native")
xn.values.shape
#> (24, 1440, 1)
f"{xn.values.nbytes / 2**20:.1f} MB"
#> 0.3 MB

# Three years of hourly readings on 894 plots, one channel, in megabytes
894 * (3 * 365 + 1) * 24 * 8 / 2**20
#> 179.4111328125

The weekly grain of the same record holds 9 bins against the 1440 of the native array, and the Schrankogel record of the package’s origin, 894 plots read hourly for three years, would be about 179 MB for a single channel. A run on a long hourly record is quickest to iterate on at a few coarse grains with n_inner = NULL, reaching for native() and the inner search once the comparison is settled. elasticnet() and forest() take threads, and what they return does not depend on it.

Two runs give different numbers

The random draws in a run come from seeds the call carries: cv(seed = ) for the outer folds, the seed of timesift() for the inner splits, and the seed of each learner that draws, such as elasticnet()’s inner cross-validation and forest()’s bootstrap. With the same seeds the same call gives the same numbers.

run <- function(seed) {
  timesift(targets, series, y = starts_with("sp"), id = plot, time = t,
           sift = grains("week", "month"), resampling = cv(v = 3, seed = seed),
           n_inner = NULL, ensemble = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
}
a <- run(1)
b <- run(1)
c2 <- run(2)
identical(a$scores, b$scores)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(a$scores, c2$scores)
#> [1] FALSE
def run(seed):
    return ts.timesift(targets, series, y="sp*", id="plot", time="t",
                       sift=ts.grains("week", "month"), resampling=ts.cv(v=3, seed=seed),
                       n_inner=None, ensemble=False, verbose=False)

a = run(1)
b = run(1)
c2 = run(2)
pd.DataFrame(a.scores).equals(pd.DataFrame(b.scores))
#> True
pd.DataFrame(a.scores).equals(pd.DataFrame(c2.scores))
#> False

The fold map draws under its own seed and puts the session’s random number stream back as it found it, so a call does not shift the draws that follow it.

y2 <- as.matrix(targets[c("sp1", "sp2")])
rownames(y2) <- targets$plot
set.seed(3); first <- runif(1)
set.seed(3); invisible(fold_map(y2, v = 3)); second <- runif(1)
identical(first, second)
#> [1] TRUE

When a rerun differs, the usual cause is a changed input: a row order, a time zone or a filter upstream. The digest of the array is a quick test of whether two runs read the same representation.

digest_array(grain_matrix(series, plot, t, temp, grain = "week"))
#> [1] "61296ebef3384a8fde101fc1540d2ae8"
digest_array(grain_matrix(series[sample(nrow(series)), ], plot, t, temp, grain = "week"))
#> [1] "61296ebef3384a8fde101fc1540d2ae8"
ts.digest_array(ts.grain_matrix(series, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week"))
#> 9337f31e937aea21c9a0f1901fe0875f
shuffled = series.sample(frac=1, random_state=1)
ts.digest_array(ts.grain_matrix(shuffled, "plot", "t", "temp", grain="week"))
#> 9337f31e937aea21c9a0f1901fe0875f

The two digests agree because the rows of a representation are sorted by unit, whatever order the series arrives in. The neural learners are seeded through train_control(seed = ), but a network trained by torch is not promised to give the same weights to the last bit on another machine or device, and the package does not test that it does.

R and Python give different numbers

The R and the Python package call one compiled core, and the contract between them is written down in The representation contract. grain_matrix() and lookback_matrix() must give the same array in both, which is checked as a digest against fixtures shipped with the package. The check can be run on any installation.

fx <- system.file("spec", "fixtures", package = "timesift")
rec <- read.csv(file.path(fx, "series.csv"))
rec$time <- as.POSIXct(rec$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
expected <- read.csv(file.path(fx, "digests.csv"))
row <- expected[expected$series == "aligned" & expected$grain == "week" & expected$tz == "UTC" &
                  expected$year_start == "09-01" & expected$partial == "keep" &
                  expected$stat == "mean", ]
got <- grain_matrix(rec, id, time, value, grain = "week", year_start = "09-01")
c(expected = row$digest, got = digest_array(got))
#>                           expected                                got 
#> "23015e94770e53ec80212f6e756f96bf" "23015e94770e53ec80212f6e756f96bf"

The elastic net is pinned as a distance rather than a digest: two coordinate descents stop at the same point to the tolerance they are run at and no closer, so its coefficients agree to that tolerance. Neural networks trained by R’s torch and Python’s are not required to agree beyond what two seeds of one network would. A difference in a representation digest, or in a penalised fit beyond its tolerance, is a bug in whichever language changed, and worth reporting.

The more common source of disagreement is the input. R sorts units in C collation, as NumPy does, but a time column parsed in different zones in the two languages bins on different calendars, and a year_start set on one side only moves every season and year.

Questions that come up

Does timesift standardise the readings?

Not in the representation. grain_matrix() returns the readings in their own units, because a scale computed over all units would carry the held-out units into the input. The neural encoders standardise each channel over the units each network is fitted on.

Can units cover different periods?

Not on a calendar grain, where every unit must reach every bin. A target with an instant of its own, such as a survey date, is read with a lookback() and target_time, and then only the span before each target has to be covered.

Are columns of targets used as predictors automatically?

No. A column that is neither the response, the identifier nor target_time is ignored unless static names it.

Which number goes in a paper?

fit$estimate, the held-out score of the selection and the stack. The highest candidate mean in fit$candidates was picked on the same folds it is scored on.

Why is a response missing from the scores?

Its cells are not scorable under the fold map, and fit$cells says which and why.

Which candidates were skipped?

Those with status “not applicable” in fit$candidates, with the reason in note.

Can a fit be saved and used in another session?

Yes. A fit is a plain list, and a fitted encoder holds its weights as arrays, so saveRDS() and readRDS() round trip it and it predicts on another machine. A learner registered with register_learner() has to be registered again before predicting.

What does grains("auto") choose?

Every named grain the record gives at least two bins.

Reporting a bug

A refusal that names the wrong cause, a digest that disagrees with the fixtures, or a result that changes between two runs with the same seeds is worth an issue at https://github.com/gcol33/timesift/issues. The most useful report holds a small record that reproduces it, built as the tables in this article are, the output of packageVersion("timesift") and sessionInfo(), and the message as printed.
